correzioni: 14-atlante.js, intro: «un «Ciao, mondo» per ciascuno» changed to «per quasi tutti, un «Ciao, mondo»». In the lab, 4 languages have no hello world (Short Code, Autocode, ALGOL 58, CPL) and 2 have only a fragment (Plankalkül, FLOW-MATIC).

14-atlante.js, «Come si legge la mappa»: the Plankalkül exception now comes straight after the sentence about years that it qualifies. Before, it followed the sentence about the curves, so it was unclear what it was an exception to.

14-atlante.js: «un compilatore o un interprete traduce ogni programma nel codice macchina» was wrong for interpreters, which run a program rather than translate it. It now reads: «a girare è sempre il codice macchina… un compilatore vi traduce il programma una volta per tutte, oppure un interprete, che è a sua volta un programma in codice macchina, lo esegue un'istruzione alla volta». This matches the wording of chapters 4 and 13.

14-atlante.js, Backus paragraph: the loose paraphrase «un'assegnazione è una parola che viaggia…» is replaced with one faithful to the 1977 lecture. Variables mimic memory cells, assignments mimic data moving one word at a time along the narrow channel he named «collo di bottiglia di von Neumann».

14-atlante.js, Perlis epigram 19 («A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not worth knowing»): the Italian had a dangling subject. It is now «Un linguaggio che non influisce sul tuo modo di pensare la programmazione non merita di essere conosciuto». «il primo premio Turing» became «il primo a ricevere il premio Turing, nel 1966», and «lo scrisse» became «ne spiegò il perché».
14-atlante.js, table: «senza salti» → «senza salti arbitrari»; «senza modificare i dati» → «evitando di modificare i dati». This is more accurate and matches the lab's paradigm descriptions.
14-atlante.js, table caption: Rust replaced by Kotlin among languages that mix «istruzioni, oggetti e funzioni», because Rust has no classes or objects in the usual sense.
14-atlante.js, sapevi: SOL is spelled out (Simple Object Language), and the text now says that *sol* means «sole» in Portuguese. Confirmed by searches pointing to lua.org.

14-atlante.js, glossary entry «programmazione funzionale»: «Nasce con il LISP… Haskell ne è l'esempio più rigoroso» (an opinion) → «Il LISP (1958) ne è il capostipite, Haskell (1990) il più noto dei linguaggi funzionali «puri»».

14-atlante.js, fonti: the Lua source cited a non-existent title, «A Brief History of Lua», at lua.org/history.html, which is actually the 2001 SBLP paper. It now cites «The Evolution of Lua», HOPL III 2007, https://www.lua.org/doc/hopl.pdf.

14-atlante.js, fonti: the Kernighan B tutorial URL is updated to https://www.nokia.com/bell-labs/about/dennis-m-ritchie/btut.html, and the date is now «1972 o 1973 (le fonti non concordano)». The Perlis URL is now https://cs.yale.edu/homes/perlis-alan/quotes.html (confirmed by search).

14-atlante.js, fonti: two sources added that support lab facts. Ungar & Smith, «Self: The Power of Simplicity», OOPSLA '87, SIGPLAN Notices 22(12), pp. 227–242. Pigott's HOPL roster at hopl.info, used for FLOW-MATIC, Brief Code and ABC. There are now 10 sources.
lab/atlante.js, Autocode: «Nel 1954 Tony Brooker…» → «Tra il 1954 e il 1955». Sources say the Mark 1 Autocode was planned in 1954 and in use from 1955.

lab/atlante.js, Short Code: now says it was first called Brief Code; the BINAC version was never debugged or tested; the UNIVAC I version followed in 1950; it ran about 50 times slower than machine code.
lab/atlante.js, FLOW-MATIC: «fu il primo…» → «è considerato il primo…», since HOPL hedges this. The year note now says that sources give 1955, 1957 or 1958 as its birth year.

lab/atlante.js, B: «il primo «hello, world» documentato» → «il più antico «hello, world» conosciuto», following Ritchie's «so far as Brian and I can remember». The hello-world note now gives the date as «1972 o 1973: le fonti non concordano».
lab/atlante.js, SQL note: «in Oracle si aggiunge FROM DUAL» was outdated, because Oracle 23 accepts SELECT without FROM. It now says «le versioni meno recenti di Oracle richiedono anche FROM DUAL».

lab/atlante.js: Common Lisp book title corrected to «Common Lisp the Language». R's name explained more precisely: the shared initial of Ross and Robert, and a nod to S. Eiffel: the name honours Gustave Eiffel.
lab/atlante.js, PL/I: «presentò nel 1964 insieme ai computer System/360» → «presentò nel 1964 per la nuova famiglia di computer System/360». The first compiler only came in 1966.
erroriFattuali: Source title invented or wrong: «A Brief History of Lua» on lua.org/history.html. That page holds a different paper (SBLP 2001). Replaced with the HOPL III paper and its correct URL.

Kernighan's B tutorial: the 1972 date was stated as certain, but sources give 1972 or 1973 (the companion B report is dated January 1973). The URL was the old bell-labs.com path, now replaced by the nokia.com address.
The intro promised a «Ciao, mondo» for every language, but 6 of the 58 have none or only a fragment.
The text said an interpreter translates every program into machine code. An interpreter runs the program; it does not translate it.
Rust was given as an example of mixing objects with other paradigms. Rust has no classes or objects in the classic sense.
Autocode: Brooker's Mark 1 Autocode was dated 1954, but sources say planned in 1954 and developed or used in 1955.
FLOW-MATIC's «fu il primo» claim was stated as fact, but HOPL says «possibly the first». Its birth year also differs by source (1955, 1957 or 1958).
B's hello world was called «il primo documentato», but the authors themselves only say «so far as we can remember». Now worded as «il più antico conosciuto».
SQL: «in Oracle si aggiunge FROM DUAL» is out of date for Oracle 23 and later.
Common Lisp: book title given wrongly as «Common Lisp: the Language»; the real title is «Common Lisp the Language».
PL/I was said to be presented «insieme ai computer System/360». It was designed for that family, but its compiler arrived only in 1966.
Glossary: «Haskell ne è l'esempio più rigoroso» was an opinion presented as fact.
problemiAperti: ALGOL 60 hello world: I could not confirm online that `outstring` is defined in the 1976 «Modified Report». From memory it is in Appendix 2, «environmental block». The lab note says only «una revisione successiva», which is safe. The double quotes follow modern compilers such as MARST; the reference language uses ‘…’.

Plankalkül snippet `V0 + V1 ⇒ R0`: a thesis on Plankalkül confirms that the arrow marks where a result goes, but no search confirmed that it is the assignment sign. The note is already worded safely (it only says the arrow shows where the result goes).
Ada: the date of MIL-STD-1815 (10 December 1980) was not confirmed online. The text only says «la prima norma è del 1980», which stands either way.

Van Roy source: the PDF and its 2009 date are confirmed. That it appeared in the IRCAM/Delatour volume *New Computational Paradigms for Computer Music* matches the usual citation, but no search confirmed it.
Backus source: journal, volume 21, issue 8 and August 1978 are confirmed. The page range 613–641 and the DOI are cited from memory.

Cross-section links (../porte-logiche/index.html, ../chip-programmabili/index.html) point to folders that do not exist yet in this repository; only sections/programmazione exists. They will work once the sections are merged, as in the other chapters.

note:
Scope: I listed and checked every claim in the chapter (intro, 2 text blocks, the lab intro, the table, sapevi, 4 glossary terms, 10 sources). In the lab I reviewed all 58 languages (year, authors, description), about 60 of the 93 influence links (all match the commonly documented «influenced by»; none goes from a younger language to an older one), and the syntax of all 52 hello worlds (all correct). I used 21 WebSearch calls (the riskiest claims first) and 1 WebFetch, which failed with a DNS error as expected.

Confirmed online:
- Backus's 1977 Turing lecture, his «von Neumann languages» and the term «von Neumann bottleneck» (CACM 21(8), August 1978).
- Perlis's Epigrams (SIGPLAN Notices 17(9), September 1982, pp. 7–13) and the Yale page.
- Lua/SOL/sun and Tecgraf.
- Short Code / Brief Code (Mauchly 1949, Schmitt, BINAC, UNIVAC 1950, about 50 times slower).
- Glennie's Autocode 1952 and Brooker's 1954–1955 version.
- FLOW-MATIC (1955–1959, HOPL dates it 1957).
- Self (designed 1986, OOPSLA 1987).
- ABC (January 1987; Geurts, Meertens, Pemberton).
- Ichbiah and the «Green» proposal at CII Honeywell Bull.
- Zig (8 February 2016).
- Logo (BBN, 1967; Feurzeig, Papert, Solomon; robot turtle 1969).
- Objective-C (1984; Cox and Love at PPI; NeXT).
- B tutorial (1972 or 1973).
- The Van Roy and Lua HOPL PDFs exist.
The remaining claims were checked against well-established knowledge and against the neighbouring chapters (unix, oggetti, logica), which agree with them.

Every lab feature the chapter describes exists in the lab: Tab/arrows/Enter/Esc, amber ancestors and blue descendants, paradigm chips, search by author (placeholder «es. Wirth»), the «Vista elenco» button, horizontal scroll on small screens, and completion after 3 languages opened. All 38 languages with a `capitolo` link are actually named in their linked chapter.
